title: Franklin Borrows a Book From a Rival
text:
In 1736 Benjamin Franklin was chosen clerk of the Pennsylvania Assembly, a post that also brought him profitable printing work for the province. The next year, when he was proposed again, a new member of the House made a long speech against him. Franklin noted that the man was wealthy, educated and likely to become influential, so his hostility was a real problem.

Franklin decided not to flatter him. Instead, he heard that the man owned a very scarce and curious book, and he wrote him a note asking to borrow it for a few days. The rival sent it at once. Franklin returned it about a week later with another note thanking him warmly for the favor.

The next time they met in the House, the man spoke to Franklin for the first time, and with great civility. In his Autobiography Franklin says the man was ready to serve him on every occasion afterward, and that they became great friends until the man's death. Franklin explained it with an old maxim: he who has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another than he whom you yourself have obliged.
lesson: To soften a cold or hostile colleague, try asking for a small, genuine favor and thanking them sincerely. People tend to like those they have helped.
